Meanwhile, Anduril is teaming up with Qualcomm to build a 90% U.S.-manufactured laptop supply chain called "Blue Chip." Oversubscribed Equity Offering: Meta has boosted its planned equity offering to almost $98 billion, with the initial $25 billion stock sale tranche...

TL;DR

Meta is raising its equity offering to nearly $98 billion to fund AI infrastructure, while Anthropic’s impending IPO reveals staggering growth alongside multi-billion-dollar losses that are testing Wall Street's appetite for pure-play generative AI. Meanwhile, Anduril is teaming up with Qualcomm to build a 90% U.S.-manufactured laptop supply chain called "Blue Chip."

Meta's $98 Billion Equity Raise & Chip Partnerships

  • Oversubscribed Equity Offering: Meta has boosted its planned equity offering to almost $98 billion, with the initial $25 billion stock sale tranche experiencing five times oversubscription.
  • Transaction Structure: The raise includes $12.5 billion in preferred shares and a $60 billion at-the-market share sale program using Class C non-voting shares.
  • Shareholder Resistance: A lawsuit has been filed against Meta and CEO Mark Zuckerberg, with critics labeling him a "boardroom bully" over the Class C stock mechanism, which critics argue provides Zuckerberg with liquidity to cover potential tax liabilities from the proposed California billionaire tax.
  • Semiconductor Integration: Major chipmakers are participating in the equity raise—NVIDIA is investing $3 billion, while AMD and Broadcom are each contributing $1 billion. Additionally, Meta has installed AMD’s rack-scale AI systems and is testing them ahead of a broader rollout.

Anthropic's IPO Filing & The Economics of AI Compute

  • Staggering S-1 Metrics: Anthropic's S-1 filing reveals revenue growth exceeding 1,000% year-over-year in 2025, driven heavily by the adoption of its automated coding agents, alongside an $8.7 billion net loss on $16.3 billion in revenue for the first six months of 2026.
  • Balance Sheet and Cash Reserves: Anthropic is sitting on $130 billion in cash and is expected to target a raise matching or exceeding SpaceX's valuation.
  • Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs): Broadcom is arranging a $63 billion deal via a new SPV with committed financing from multiple firms to purchase chips and lease them back to Anthropic, acting as an alternative funding mechanism to traditional unsecured bonds and equity.
  • Compute Cost Pressures: Compute costs account for 55% of Anthropic's revenue, and the company carries contractual commitments scaling from one year out to 20 years.

Anduril's "Blue Chip" U.S. Manufacturing Initiative

  • Supply Chain Overhaul: Anduril is partnering with Qualcomm to build "Blue Chip," a rugged computer and laptop line designed for the military, public sector, first responders, and critical infrastructure (such as medical facilities and power plants).
  • Domestic Sourcing Milestones: The laptop will be designed and assembled in the U.S., with circuit board assembly at Anduril's Ohio factory and Qualcomm chips manufactured in Arizona; the supply chain is currently about 90% U.S. and allied, with a roadmap to reach 100%.
  • Software Integration: Anduril maintains more software engineers than hardware engineers combined, utilizing its *Lattice* software platform to ensure compatibility with legacy government systems.

Financial Markets & Corporate Earnings

  • SoFi Q3 Results: SoFi reported its strongest quarter yet with 44% year-over-year revenue growth, driven by a 44% jump in product growth and an expanded member base.
  • Diversification & Margins: Non-lending products now represent 87% of SoFi's offerings, with eight distinct businesses generating over $100 million in annual revenue and a net income margin of 17% for the quarter.
  • Sector Performance: Semiconductor and technology stocks outperformed for the third consecutive session, buoyed by positive market reactions to frontier lab IPO filings.

AI-Generated Political Advertising & Tech News Roundup

  • Midterm Ad Spend: The Wesleyan Media Project found that over $137 million has been spent on AI-generated political ads across more than 220 tracked ads.
  • Partisan Discrepancy & Disclaimers: More than 80% of detected AI political ads originate from Republican sponsors, and over 70% of those identified AI ads lack any disclosure disclaimer.
  • Industry Developments:
    • Intel agreed to buy an Israeli quantum computing startup for approximately $2.3 billion, aiming to close the deal in the first half of next year.
    • Apple acknowledged a display inner-screen cracking issue on a small number of new iPhone Duos and is offering replacements via Apple Care, while unveiling new 24-inch iMacs and entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pros featuring Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 starting at $1,500 and just under $2,000 respectively.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Mandeep Singh: Meta will successfully execute its fundraising ahead of the Anthropic IPO to capitalize on strong market demand for consumer-facing agentic AI models.
  • Palmer Luckey: Anduril will make further announcements regarding U.S. display panel vendor partnerships in 2027, potentially at CES.
  • Palmer Luckey: Anduril's Blue Chip laptop will enter full production next year.

Notable Quotes

*"When you're talking about $98 billion in potential equity raise, this is still a small amount. 5% to 6% of the overall equity raise, but there's no doubt that the optics aren't great."* — Mandeep Singh

NYSE Texas President & AT&T on Dual Listings

TL;DR: AT&T and NYSE Texas highlight the strategic advantages of dual listings and Texas's booming capital markets, positioning the region as a growing hub for corporate headquarters, startups, and established enterprises alike.

The Competitive Exchange Landscape in Texas

  • Market Dynamics:
    • Exchange Competition: Bryan Daniel notes that while competition among exchanges in Dallas and Texas is fierce, it mirrors historical regional competition and drives innovation rather than constituting an all-out "exchange war."
    • Rival Exchange Activity: A handful of companies (including Energy Transfer, Sunoco, and Dillard's) have transferred primary listings to rival exchanges, while Schwab maintains a secondary listing. Daniel emphasizes that issuers make independent decisions based on individual relationships and needs.
  • NYSE Texas Scale:
    • Current Footprint: NYSE Texas currently boasts 133 dual listings, comprising a mix of corporate issuers and ETFs.
    • Proven Infrastructure: Bryan Daniel stresses that NYSE Texas leverages a 200+ year-old battle-tested computing and trading model, distinguishing it from early-stage startup exchanges relying on regulatory cash incentives and fee credits.

AT&T's Dual Listing and Milestone Year

  • Founding Class Participation:
    • No-Brainer Decision: Brett Feldman shares that AT&T joined NYSE Texas as part of its founding class because the dual-listing process required zero cost, no incremental obligations, and minimal paperwork with full support from the NYSE group.
    • Landmark History: The move coincides with AT&T's milestone year: the 150th anniversary of the first phone call (celebrated at the NYSE) and the 125th year of AT&T's listing on the NYSE.
  • Strategic Rationale for Dual Listings:
    • Amplified Footprint: Bryan Daniel explains that dual listings allow established companies to maintain their primary New York Stock Exchange experience while enhancing their visibility, workforce, customer base, or investor presence specifically in Texas.
    • Anticipating the Hub: Brett Feldman notes that while the exact long-term financial benefits are still unfolding, AT&T wanted to get in on the front end of Texas becoming a major listing hub.

Corporate Governance and State Regulatory Environment

  • NYSE Philosophy:
    • Board Autonomy: Bryan Daniel states that the NYSE group has never attempted to dictate corporate governance outcomes, leaving those decisions entirely up company boards and C-suites.
  • Texas Regulatory Appeal:
    • Lighter Touch: Discussions surrounding state-level regulatory environments focus on offering companies maximum freedom to select structures that work best for their customers and communities.

TL;DR

Oracle and OpenAI announced an expanded partnership at Oracle AI World integrating ChatGPT and Codex into Oracle's software and infrastructure, while showcasing new products across media, security, infrastructure, and data platforms.

Media Fabric & Adaptive Platform

  • Oracle Media Fabric: Designed to fundamentally change media creation, delivery, and experience through a unified suite of tools.
      • Creative Studio: Reimagines production workflows using Oracle's AI media models (supporting still images, video generation, and IP rights management) alongside other leading third-party models.
      • Video Edge: Content delivery system featuring edge compute for content optimization and generation, optimized by the emerging "media over quick" open standard.
      • Adaptive Media Platform: Combines Creative Studio and Video Edge to deliver real-time ad personalization and interactive live viewing experiences at scale.
  • Availability: Currently in limited availability with key customers, with general launch scheduled for early next year.

Security, Authentication & AI Security Mesh

  • Evolution of Security Risks:
      • Initial LLM deployments faced prompt injection and data disclosure risks.
      • AI-written code introduced supply chain risks, including malicious packages targeting build systems.
      • Strict sandboxing models introduced too much developer friction until vendor-backed enterprise controls were adopted.
  • Biometric Authentication: Added facial, voice, and fingerprint recognition to Oracle Identity and Access Management to verify human-in-the-loop approvals.
  • Agentic Identity & Access Control: Introduced agent identity management supporting rapid creation/deletion, minimal just-in-time access, and specific approval workflows.
  • Oracle AI Security Mesh: A new product enabling companies to use advanced cyber models to continuously discover system vulnerabilities, test attack paths, and deploy automated fixes.
  • Rob Clark's Perspective: Noted that AI is not creating bugs but rather helping uncover decades-old security issues, predicting fewer patches and more secure software over the long term.

Infrastructure, Accelerators & Power Management

  • AI Accelerators & Hardware Integration:
      • Nvidia Systems: Spans from P100 (2017) and H100 (2023) to Grace Blackwell rack-scale compute with NVLink, alongside delivery of the first Vera Rubin systems to customers.
      • Alternative Processors: Bringing Google TPUs (starting with TPU V8) to OCI, AMD MI300 and 455 rack-scale offerings, Positron Atlas (power-efficient inferencing), Broadcom-OpenAI co-designed Jalapeno chips, and Cerebus/Samonova low-latency inferencing.
  • Acceleron Networking: Features multi-planar front-end and back-end networks that provide full redundancy, higher resiliency, and RDMA over front-end networks.
  • Storage Partnerships: First-party NetApp integration in OCI alongside a partner program for AI-accelerated storage (Weta, Vast, DDN) connected via Acceleron and RDMA.
  • Power Infrastructure & Grid Stability:
      • Praep Vincent highlighted that AI clusters act as massive, highly coordinated electrical loads.
      • Utilizes large energy stores (batteries and supercapacitors) combined with sophisticated power electronics as a "giant shock absorber" to smooth out power ramps and prevent grid destabilization.

Data Ecosystem, Apex & Enterprise Workflows

  • Deep Trust AI Architecture: Pushes data controls down into the database to individual tables, rows, and columns for automated policy enforcement regardless of user or agent.
  • Oracle Apex & Apex Lang: Distills enterprise applications into a high-level language ("Apex Lang") that allows AI coding agents to build applications within a safe, governed, Oracle-maintained runtime.
  • Oracle App Composer: Combines Codex code generation with IT governance, profiles, and deployment controls to turn business ideas into enterprise applications.
  • Oracle AI Workspace: Developed in partnership with OpenAI, it unifies Oracle and third-party data (Slack, Office 365, wikis) to answer questions and drive complex workflows across the enterprise.
  • Startup Bundle: Combines NetSuite QuickStart financial software, OCI credits, and OpenAI credits for new businesses.

Partnership Insights: Clay Magourk & Sam Altman

  • Model Adoption & Productivity:
      • Sam Altman noted that GPT-6 adoption has been OpenAI's strongest ever, advancing rapidly from grade school math to hard unproven math problems and enterprise software generation.
      • Clay Magourk shared that more than 70% of Oracle's software is now written by AI via Codex.
      • Altman described the modern developer experience as managing a factory inside a computer, unlocking software creation for non-technical workers.
  • AI-Driven Innovation: Altman highlighted that AI is accelerating scientific discovery and hardware design, noting that OpenAI used AI to design the Jalapeno chip faster than previously imaginable.

Notable Quotes

*"The last six months have felt like a very accelerated version... GPT-6 was one of those moments where I think the models took a step forward all at once both in terms of their ability to discover new knowledge to do very hard things but also for people's ability to work with the models."* — Sam Altman
*"My experience now sitting in front of a computer using the latest tools is... like I am managing a factory inside of my computer and I can get things that I don't enjoy doing to be automated."* — Sam Altman
*"AI is not creating the problem. AI is not creating these bugs. AI is helping us discover all of the security issues that we've have developed over the past 50 years."* — Clay Magourk

Prediction Market Betting Stretches Past Sports

Bloomberg Podcasts(603.0K)·12:49·744 views·2026-10-27
Sean Patrick MaloneyCEO and President, Coalition for Prediction Markets
TL;DRPrediction markets are expanding rapidly beyond sports and politics into financial indices, offering a transparent, market-driven forecasting tool that the Coalition for Prediction Markets argues should be regulated federally as financial derivatives rather than casinos.
Intersection of Tech and Finance: Sean Patrick Maloney joined as CEO and President of the Coalition for Prediction Markets in January because the industry sits at the intersection of technology, public affairs, and financial markets. Maloney previously ran a derivative...
  • TL;DR: Prediction markets are expanding rapidly beyond sports and politics into financial indices, offering a transparent, market-driven forecasting tool that the Coalition for Prediction Markets argues should be regulated federally as financial derivatives rather than casinos.

Industry Role and the Rise of Prediction Markets

  • Intersection of Tech and Finance:
    • Sean Patrick Maloney joined as CEO and President of the Coalition for Prediction Markets in January because the industry sits at the intersection of technology, public affairs, and financial markets.
    • Maloney previously ran a derivative software risk management company and chaired the congressional committee overseeing the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) for 10 years.
  • Information Source and Forecasting:
    • Prediction markets function as a nonpartisan, real-time, unbiased source of information to help make sense of chaotic events like Senate races.
    • Approximately 75% of people accessing these platforms do not trade at all, using them purely as a forecasting tool to view crowd-sourced probabilities.
  • Accuracy and Limitations:
    • While polls are biased, expensive, and infrequent, prediction markets rely on the "wisdom of markets" and liquidity.
    • Maloney acknowledges they are not perfect—noting they got the Brazil election wrong in the first round, just as initial voters did—comparing them to autonomous driving technology that only needs to outperform human alternatives.

Regulatory Framework and Market Integrity

  • Federal vs. State Oversight:
    • Maloney emphasizes that he exclusively represents US-based, federally regulated prediction market platforms such as Kalshi, Robinhood, Coinbase, Crypto.com, and Underdog.
    • These platforms play by standard US financial market rules and should be overseen by a well-funded CFTC rather than state gaming commissions.
  • Assessment of the CFTC:
    • Maloney defends the CFTC as a major federal regulator handling a half a trillion dollars of notional derivatives volume annually, though he agrees it requires proper staffing, commissioners in their seats, and a robust enforcement budget.
    • The CFTC is currently undergoing a rule-making process to address concerns in prediction markets, which Maloney's coalition fully supports.

Preventing Market Manipulation and Insider Trading

  • Built-In Market Disincentives:
    • Financial markets inherently punish bad actors trying to manipulate prices because opposing traders have "skin in the game" and deep knowledge.
  • State-of-the-Art Surveillance:
    • Platforms employ advanced tech like IC360 and sophisticated surveillance programs under the hood to proactively block insiders before they trade.
    • For example, members of Congress and their staff, as well as individuals working for sports teams, are proactively blocked from trading on Kalshi.
  • Law Enforcement Collaboration:
    • Bad actors who attempt manipulation are investigated, referred to law enforcement, and prosecuted.
    • Maloney stresses that platform business models rely on integrity and trustworthiness to succeed.

Sports Contracts vs. Casino Betting

  • Derivatives vs. House-Backed Gambling:
    • Critics question the high volume of sports-related wagering on prediction platforms, viewing it as sports betting.
    • Maloney argues that a derivatives market—where peers trade as counterparties on a neutral exchange with a small fee—differs fundamentally from a casino business model where the "house wins when you lose," or sports books that ban winning players.
  • Consumer Preference:
    • Tens of millions of consumers prefer the derivatives market approach over traditional casinos where odds are set by the house.
  • Availability in Prohibited States:
    • Platforms like Kalshi allow users in states like California (where sports books are illegal) to trade event contracts, just as residents can trade any other financial market.

Demographics, Age Limits, and Responsible Usage

  • Standard Financial Age Rules:
    • Age restrictions on prediction platforms match those of standard financial markets (such as buying stocks or options).
  • Trading Volume Demographics:
    • 97% of trading volume on Kalshi comes from users aged 21 and up, leaving users aged 18 to 20 representing a very small percentage of activity.
  • New Safeguards:
    • Kalshi announced proactive measures to encourage responsible usage, including deposit limits over specific time periods and proactive messaging regarding portfolio trade sizing.
  • Offshore Risk:
    • Restricting access to regulated US platforms that care about user protection will only drive users to offshore platforms accessed via VPNs.

Expansion Beyond Sports

  • Growth Trajectory:
    • Non-sports categories are experiencing higher growth multiples compared to sports, akin to Amazon's early days when skeptics asked why it was only about books.
  • New Financial Partnerships:
    • Kalshi announced a partnership with the Dow and the S&P 500 to introduce new index-based products, signaling a major expansion into financial market disruption and use cases far removed from sports.

Previewing the Fed Meeting and AI IPOs | Bloomberg Surveillance

TL;DR

Markets face an "uncomfortable sweet spot" characterized by strong AI-driven growth alongside high structural deficits, debt leverage, and rising yields, with experts weighing risks of deceleration, a crowded AI capex cycle, and the upcoming midterm elections.

Economic Outlook & Fiscal Policy

  • Robert Kaplan on US Growth Dynamics:
    • The economy is super strong in AI-related and defense sectors, but sluggish in housing, autos, and serving lower-middle-income consumers.
    • Inflation is largely structural rather than cyclical, driven heavily by energy costs like elevated diesel prices embedded across 50 items.
    • Recommends the Fed debate how much current inflation is supply-driven versus demand-driven rather than acting as if the economy is simply overheating.
  • Fiscal Deficits & Government Leverage:
    • Governments globally are highly leveraged in the aftermath of COVID, pushing the Treasury curve to act poorly as a cyclical diversifier.
    • Robert Kaplan's Reform Menu: Advocates addressing long-term debt through immigration reform (bringing in 1–2 million workers annually to fill open jobs), balanced regulation, reinstituted embedded cost management, and entitlement reform.
    • Notes that the 2026 budget deficit miss included a $250 billion entitlement surprise heading north and $100 billion in interest expense.
  • Colin Graham on Nominal Growth & Global Divergence:
    • High nominal GDP growth in the US has allowed sectors like UPS and consumers to generate good earnings, but fiscal stimulus will likely decline next year and deflate nominal GDP.
    • Europe—specifically France—lacks the US growth buffer, suffering from tight ECB monetary conditions and an acute energy shock where economic growth cannot cover interest costs.

AI Infrastructure Boom & Financial Stability Risks

  • Gary Gensler on Financial and Technology Risks:
    • The AI infrastructure boom has raised over $500 billion in new debt this year, alongside a $63 billion Broadcom deal, pushing total new debt near $600 billion.
    • Warns that the insurance sector is increasingly holding this debt through private credit or direct exposure.
    • Highlights off-balance-sheet guarantees written into data centers by Broadcom, NVIDIA, and AMD via special purpose vehicles that rival past financial engineering.
  • Technology Obsolescence & Corporate Adoption:
    • Gary Gensler: Expresses uncertainty regarding the depreciation and obsolescence of memory and processor chips, noting that chips built in 2026 may lose significant value by 2032 due to rapid scaling and technological advances.
    • Robert Kaplan: Estimates that out of 2% real GDP growth, roughly half may be related to AI, warning that a roll-over in this narrow adoption wave could severely impact the broader economy.

Equity Markets & Multi-Asset Strategy

  • Mike Wilson on S&P 500 Valuations and Corrections:
    • The market has experienced a significant correction under the surface since June, which is currently 80-90% done (in the 9th inning).
    • The S&P 500 multiple has compressed by nearly 20% from a year ago (down from 23x to 18-19x earnings), successfully discounting growth deceleration.
    • Advises staying on board with quality factors and leaders rather than just the Magnificent 7, noting that strong underlying earnings growth will face tougher comps next year.
  • Colin Graham on Asset Allocation:
    • Fixed income offers limited upside with a 5% return compared to equities delivering 20% from earnings growth.
    • Currency dynamics show a stronger dollar concentrates growth in the US while keeping a floor on market volatility.

Workplace Culture & Human Capital

  • In-Office Mandates vs. Remote Work:
    • Robert Kaplan: Argues that remote work causes training, mentoring, coaching, and relationship-building skills to atrophy, making in-person gathering at firms like Goldman Sachs essential for professional development.
    • Gary Gensler: Notes that while 98% of MIT students and faculty utilize AI, users must actively train their cognitive faculties to avoid "cognitive decline" from offloading critical thinking entirely to automated tools.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Robert Kaplan: The Fed should skip a rate cut/hike today and raise rates deliberately, acknowledging that the data leaves much unknown.
  • Robert Kaplan: The AI adoption phase will fundamentally change the employment mix, resulting in fewer programmers and more client-facing, relationship-building personnel.
  • Gary Gensler: The Federal Reserve might pause its rate path after a potential December move.
  • Mike Wilson: The current under-the-surface equity correction is in its 9th inning and will conclude with clearing events like the midterm elections, allowing the bull market to advance into 2027.

Notable Quotes

"If I thought this was a cyclical overheating, I’d say, 'Let’s get moving faster.' But... the impact of raising too far or too fast may be to slow already sluggish parts of the economy, and it may not make a dent in inflation." — Robert Kaplan
"We've raised over 500 billion dollars of new debt this year and then you add this Broadcom 63 billion. So we're pushing 600 billion. And who holds it? I think it's insurance sector I worry about that's picked up a lot of holding of debt through private credit or just directly." — Gary Gensler
"Don't tell me that the market isn't paying attention. It is. The question is, is that enough of a discount? I think the multiple now is cheap enough to, to basically feel comfortable that it's discounted a lot of these risks." — Mike Wilson

Property Play: How Green Financing Is Reshaping Real Estate

TL;DR

C-PACE (Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy) financing provides commercial real estate owners with long-term, fixed-rate capital tied to energy efficiency and climate resilience that runs with the land, helping borrowers navigate a $1 trillion debt maturity wall and rising interest rates.

What is C-PACE Financing?

  • Definition and Mechanism: C-PACE (Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy) is a state-level policy enabling commercial property owners to create a voluntary special tax assessment district on their own property to secure long-term financing for energy efficiency, solar panels, and extreme weather resiliency upgrades.
  • Deal Flexibility: Flexible Capital Stack Integration: The financing can be used to take out construction financing on recently completed upgrades, fund new property construction (securing more capital by outperforming energy code), or retrofit existing properties.
  • Senior Security: Runs with the Land: C-PACE assessments survive bankruptcies and foreclosures, staying attached to the property even if sold, which provides the long-dated, highly secure assets sought by institutional investors.

Company Growth & Scale (Nuveen Green Capital)

  • AUM Expansion: $7 Billion AUM: Nuveen Green Capital grew from $300 million in assets under management at the time of its 2021 acquisition by Nuveen up to $7 billion to date.
  • Geographic Reach: 40 States: The company expanded from operating in just three or four early states (Connecticut, Maryland, Missouri, and California in 2015) to active operations across 40 states.
  • Market Penetration: 5% of CMBS Market: Annual C-PACE issuances currently represent about 5% of the annual Commercial Mortgage-Backed Securities (CMBS) market.
  • Team & Structure: Over 100 Employees: The company employs more than 100 people and maintains an average senior team tenure of eight years within an 11-year-old industry.

Navigating the Commercial Real Estate Crisis

  • The Maturity Wall: $1 Trillion Debt Wall: The commercial real estate market faces a $1 trillion maturity wall driven by bank-funded short-term loans requiring balloon payments every 5, 7, or 10 years.
  • Refinancing Gaps: Squeezed Proceeds: Rising interest rates are depressing property values and shrinking operating margins, meaning mortgage proceeds available during refinancing are frequently lower than the original loans from 2021 or 2022.
  • Risk Mitigation: Long-Term Debt Tool: Borrowers use C-PACE as a risk-mitigation tool to inject equity and secure long-term fixed-rate debt for a portion of their capital stack so they avoid refinancing risks every five years.
  • Sector Agnosticism: All Major Asset Classes: The firm lends across all major asset classes—including office buildings in San Francisco post-COVID and struggling hotels requiring stabilization—by underwriting based on long-term property location and use rather than specific property themes.

Investor Base & Capital Strategy

  • Primary Lenders: Life Insurance Companies: Capital is sourced primarily from insurance companies, including general account TIAA-CREF and international life insurance companies in Asia, due to their appetite for long-dated, secure investments.
  • Exclusion of Private Equity Capital: Direct Insurance Execution: Private equity firms have shown interest in buying the platform, but direct execution with insurance companies remains the best method for providing long-term capital.
  • Historical Milestones: 2017 Securitization: Greenworks Lending (founded in 2015) executed the asset class's first securitization in 2017, with Nuveen acting as the sole note purchaser before acquiring the company in 2021.

Leadership & Organizational Culture

  • Management Philosophy: Radical Candor & Psychological Safety: Ally Cooley applies principles from Kim Scott’s book *Radical Candor*—focusing on psychological safety and knowing team members' backgrounds and career goals—to achieve high staff retention.
  • Parental Transparency: Humanizing Leadership: Cooley openly shares her experiences as a mother of three daughters, modeling work-life trade-offs to foster an open, supportive corporate culture.
  • Nuveen Integration: Autonomous Subsidiary: Despite initial concerns about corporate absorption, Nuveen has maintained a respectful approach to Nuveen Green Capital's investment process and risk management layers while supporting its growth.

TL;DR

Despite macroeconomic headwinds like higher construction costs, interest rates, and localized office vacancies, Texas commercial real estate leadership remains overwhelmingly optimistic due to strong underlying fundamentals, accelerating corporate relocation velocity, and massive secular demand for digital and residential infrastructure.

Texas Commercial Market Dynamics & Corporate Migration

  • Shifting Corporate Footprints:
    • Torrey Littlejohn noted that while Texas recorded 25 corporate headquarters moves this year—the lowest since 2017—the state is experiencing unprecedented velocity in companies establishing new footprints with 50, 100, or 200 employees to test the market before growing exponentially.
    • Companies initially evaluate 3 to 4 submarkets before narrowing down to 1 or 2 ecosystems that seamlessly accommodate both front and back offices.
  • The Urban Core vs. Suburban Barbell:
    • Downtown Dallas is experiencing positive momentum through residential population growth, new grocery stores, restaurants, and spillover activity from Uptown and the Arts District, despite older, obsolete buildings requiring capital investment.
    • Northern suburbs like Plano and Frisco have developed distinct centers of gravity, creating a balanced "barbell" ecosystem where residents have access to diverse school districts and localized amenities without needing to visit downtown daily.

Data Centers & Digital Infrastructure

  • The Public Relations vs. Reality Gap:
    • Laura Hines-Pierce described the conversation around data centers and digital infrastructure as overly polarized ("black and white"), noting a critical need for balanced community investment covering housing, social, and physical infrastructure.
    • Michael Hyun agreed that data centers have briefly become a "four letter word" in an election year, requiring a pivot toward enhanced community engagement and better-designed, architecturally integrated facilities that avoid looking like landed "Star Wars" ships.
  • Capital Competition & Constraints:
    • Data center developments are soaking up massive amounts of debt and equity capital, competing with traditional real estate asset classes (like office, retail, and multifamily) as well as long-dated government bonds (with data center bond issuance reaching 68% of long-dated government treasuries over the past year).
    • Data center builds compete directly with traditional real estate for labor and supply, specifically driving up costs for construction contractors.

Multifamily, Housing, and Residential Master-Planned Communities

  • Multifamily Supply Cycles:
    • Michael Hyun characterized multifamily today as "the office of today"—following the previous retail cycle—driven by oversupply resulting from low interest rates 5 years ago (when 5 and 10-year rates were 350 basis points lower).
    • Multifamily is currently experiencing decade-low starts and supply, with market pain expected to persist for the next 10 to 24 months before returning to equilibrium.
  • Single-Family & Master-Planned Demand:
    • Laura Hines-Pierce highlighted that Hines' highest conviction sector is living/residential, driven by a global under-supply of over 6 million units and a 2025 influx of 400,000 people moving to Texas.
    • Crow Holdings and Hines are actively expanding lot-development platforms nationally (such as Hines' delivery of 50,000 lots) to bridge the gap for homebuilders serving millennials seeking single-family master-planned communities.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Michael Hyun predicts that multifamily market pain and oversupply distress will last for at least the next 10 to 12 to 24 months before the sector reorganizes.
  • Michael Hyun predicts that state-level regulatory frameworks for data centers will change to mandate deeper community engagement, noting that while growth may slow down temporarily, Texas will remain a winner in data center CapEx spend due to its business-friendly environment.
  • Michael Hyun predicts that total state-level bans or halts on data center development will not happen because doing so would be "economic suicide" for the Texas economy.

Notable Quotes

"Multifamily today is off is the office of today just like it was here before that. It was retail. And uh, in five years it'll be something else because all of these sectors cycle." — Michael Hyun
"Data centers don't need to be a Star Wars ship that has landed in the middle of a community. ... There's an opportunity to deliver a better financial product that leases faster, stays leased longer and gets higher rental rates, but is also an investment in the community." — Laura Hines-Pierce
"If there is a significant slowdown in that data center development, that impacts so many areas of the Texas economy... your will then require less natural gas. That will impact the the energy markets, of which Houston and Texas broadly is exposed to." — Michael Hyun

TL;DR

The Texas Stock Exchange (TXSE) has raised $440 million in total equity backing—including a newly announced investment from State Street—and surpassed $300 billion in listings within its first 22 days of trading. CEO James Lee argues that the 30-year listing duopoly of NYSE and Nasdaq is over, driven by a mission to reduce regulatory and legal frictions for public companies.

Market Context & The Public Company Decline

  • Shrinking Public Markets: James Lee noted that the U.S. has half the number of public companies it had at its peak 30 years ago (dropping to around 8,100), despite record-high indices.
  • The IPO Backlog: James Lee stated there are currently 31,000 sponsor-backed companies stuck in a heavily backlogged pipeline, representing $4 trillion of marks on sponsors' books. At current exit rates, clearing this backlog will take 9.5 years.
  • Larger Issuance Sizes: James Lee highlighted that today's average IPO market cap at issuance is $2.5 billion—four times larger than 20–23 years ago—meaning everyday investors miss out on the steepest parts of growth curves.
  • Burdensome Disclosures: James Lee contrasted historical prospectuses with modern filings, noting that Anthropic’s recent filing featured a 400-page prospectus with 100 pages dedicated entirely to risk disclosures.

TXSE Capital, Backing, & Ownership

  • Breaking News - State Street Investment: James Lee announced that State Street has joined TXSE with a significant equity investment, bringing total equity capital to $440 million—an unprecedented amount for an exchange applying for SEC registration.
  • Institutional Backing: James Lee detailed that TXSE’s ownership structure includes BlackRock, Vanguard, JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs, and Bank of America.
  • Liquidity Provider Support: James Lee reported that 9 of the top 10 U.S. liquidity providers (representing 90% of daily U.S. equity volume) are equity holders in TXSE.
  • Underwriting & ETF Concentration: James Lee noted that equity holders include lead bookrunners for 91% of IPO proceeds over the last 5 years, and sponsors representing two-thirds of the nation's $17 trillion in ETF assets.

Exchange Competition & Market Fragmentation

  • End of the Duopoly: James Lee declared that the day of a listing duopoly (Nasdaq and NYSE) is over, establishing TXSE as the third registered listing exchange in the U.S.
  • Trading vs. Listing Disconnect: James Lee addressed concerns about startups lacking track records by explaining that under the National Market System (Reg NMS), there is no longer a correlation between where a company lists and where it trades. Intraday volume for NYSE-listed companies is only 8–9%, with 50% of U.S. volume occurring off-exchange across 20 exchanges and 200 venues.
  • Strict Listing Standards: James Lee emphasized that TXSE has not relaxed standards, adopting quantitative standards higher than its competitors, rendering nearly 35% of current U.S. public corporates ineligible to transfer to TXSE.

Legal Jurisdictions & Regulatory Alignment

  • The Texas Legal Exodus: James Lee pointed to major companies re-domiciling into Texas—including Tesla, Coinbase, SpaceX, Dillard's, and Exxon (which moved from New Jersey after 144 years on May 27)—creating a viable alternative to Delaware.
  • Quantifiable Cost Reductions: James Lee stated that a standard Fortune 100 company reorganizing into Texas and listing on TXSE can reduce cost structures by tens of millions of dollars annually in insurance savings, franchise taxes, and proxy preparation.
  • Regulatory Tailwinds: James Lee praised current SEC leadership for unravelling reporting apparatus costs, noting the repeal of climate disclosure mandates and the movement to rescind Rule 14a-8 regarding shareholder proposals, aligning with Texas state legislative models like SB 1057.

Issuer-Aligned Economics

  • Transparent Revenue Sharing: James Lee explained that TXSE’s financial model is entirely issuer-aligned, sharing overall economics (such as market data, corporate actions, and auction revenues) so that public companies experience a net-positive cash relationship rather than just paying opaque listing fees.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Regulatory Timeline: SEC Chairman Atkins will ring the bell at TXSE on Friday and host a roundtable to discuss state competition and making IPOs great again in America — James Lee
  • Upcoming Listings: Several companies will list on TXSE next week, and the pipeline is full — James Lee

Notable Quotes

*"The day of a listing duopoly is over. That's ended. And now there are three established listing exchanges in the United States."* — James Lee
*"If you look, uh, despite hitting new highs in the indices... the fact is we have half the number of public companies in this country that we had at the peak at 8,100 public companies 30 years ago."* — James Lee
*"There is no nexus between where you trade and where you list... 90% of your trading volume takes place off exchange."* — James Lee

I mean, it has been remarkable to look at the growth of see, just, you know, in a short order of months. And I wonder how you see it, this idea that it has been decades where the dominant exchanges have been NASDAQ and the NYSE in your mind, just how big of a challenge are you to the current regime that exists of exchanges? Well, I think if you look back over the last 20, 22 days, we've we've put up over $300 billion of listings on our exchange. So, there's some degree of competition that that's merge. The AI Boom Will Pull Back, Warns Former SEC Chair Gary Gensler

TL;DR: Former SEC Chair Gary Gensler warns that the AI investment boom is a late-stage capital expenditure cycle heading for a deceleration and reversal within 18 to 30 months, with potential financial stability risks tied to over $600 billion in new debt, off-balance-sheet guarantees, and rapid chip obsolescence.

AI Boom, Capital Exuberance, and Overbuilding

  • Historical Parallels: AI investment mirrors past overfunded capital cycles like railroads, canals, and the internet.
    • Capital Scale: Companies are raising massive sums, such as Meta's $90 billion equity offering and Broadcom's recent $63 billion package.
    • Off-Balance-Sheet Risk: Broadcom, Nvidia, and AMD are utilizing complex guarantees and setting up special purpose vehicles reminiscent of pre-2008 financial structures, sparking concerns similar to the "08 off-balance-sheet craze."
  • Hardware Depreciation: The heavy funding is concentrated in memory chips and hardware with useful lives of 4 to 7 years.
    • Due to rapid scaling and technological advances, chips built in 2026 risk losing substantial value by 2032.
  • Productivity vs. Labor Disruptions: MIT faculty hold diverse views on AI, ranging from expectations of modest productivity gains alongside labor disruptions to optimism about broader productivity gains over the next 5 to 10 years, even amid data center overbuilding.

Financial Stability and Shadow Debt Risks

  • Insurance Sector Exposure: Over $500 billion in new debt has been raised this year for AI, pushing near $600 billion when factoring in Broadcom's $63 billion package.
    • Holding Risk: The insurance sector has heavily picked up this debt either directly or through private credit.
  • Regulatory Approach: The U.S. capital markets successfully maintain a merit-neutral stance, allowing public investment in companies like Anthropic provided there are material disclosures of all risks.
  • Central Bank Implications: The Federal Reserve must factor a potential AI deceleration into future inflation and growth projections for 2027 and 2028.

Monetary Policy and Macroeconomic Outlook

  • Federal Reserve Path: Gary Gensler anticipates a rate increase in December, but questions how the Fed will adjust monetary policy afterward if a capex boom deceleration materializes, potentially leading to fewer rate hikes in 2027.
  • Nominal GDP and Fiscal Pressures: Continuous fiscal stimuli (including the Biden stimulus) risk creating pain and angst as nominal GDP growth is reined in.
  • U.S. vs. France Fiscal Room: While the U.S. possesses limited fiscal room, it is a larger and more significant economy compared to France, which faces even higher debt-to-economy ratios without the same fiscal room to intervene.

Politics, Elections, and the Next Two Years

  • Midterms and Presidential Race: The upcoming midterm elections and early 2028 presidential campaign announcements (potentially starting January or February) will shift political dynamics.
  • Lame-Duck Dynamics: History indicates presidents in their final two years turn more toward foreign affairs and hold less leverage with Congress.
    • Bipartisan Priorities: Democrats gaining leverage in the House or Senate could still collaborate with the executive branch on voter-focused issues, including affordability, housing, AI safety, and youth tech addiction.

AI and Human Cognition at MIT

  • Student Adoption: 98% of MIT graduate and undergraduate students use AI regularly, alongside faculty usage.
  • Cognitive Risks: Humans are biologically wired to conserve energy and avoid exerting their brains, creating a risk of cognitive decline if people offload critical thinking entirely to AI.
  • Critical Thinking: Success requires treating AI as a constructive bolt-on to critical thinking skills rather than a cognitive crutch.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • AI Deceleration Timeline: Gary Gensler predicts a deceleration of the AI boom followed by some form of reversal within 18 to 30 months.
  • Presidential Announcements: Gary Gensler predicts that 15 to 20 candidates for the 2028 presidential election will announce their runs by January or February of next year (or by the Wednesday after the upcoming election).
  • Federal Reserve Rate Actions: Gary Gensler predicts the Federal Reserve will implement a rate increase in December, but may slow or pause rate hikes thereafter as economic deceleration takes hold.

TL;DR

Driven by cognitive science and large language models (LLMs), Alpha School delivers core academics in just two hours a day—allowing students to learn 10 times faster while spending the rest of their day mastering real-world life skills like teamwork and entrepreneurship. In this discussion, Alpha School Principal Joe Liemandt, a16z podcast host Erik Torenberg, and Horowitz Andreessen Academy (HAA) Co-founder Gagan Biyani explore how this model is being adapted for college-age students to prioritize agency, high-ambition mentorship, and building real-world products over traditional lecture halls.

Reimagining K-12: The Alpha School Model

  • The 2-Hour Academic Engine: Traditional schooling methods have stagnated for 100 years. By leveraging modern learning science and LLMs, Alpha has engineered a system where students complete all core academics in 2 hours a day.
    • Academic Performance: Students learn twice as much as they would in a standard 6-to-7-hour school day plus homework, making them top performers on standardized tests.
    • Precision Engagement: The learning engine keeps students in an 80 to 85% correct zone, providing an unending stream of personalized lessons and scaffolding that prevents boredom or burnout.
  • Radical Student Happiness: By focusing on high standards and challenging group work, 90% of Alpha students report loving school, with 50% overall (and 65% at one specific campus) stating they would rather attend school than go on vacation.
  • Rigorous Life Skills Curriculum: The remainder of the school day is dedicated to five critical life categories: leadership/teamwork, entrepreneurship/financial literacy, socialization/relationship building, public speaking, and grit.
    • Escape Room Benchmarking: Third graders are miked up in escape rooms to measure teamwork via AI transcript analysis; students must hit 85% team-oriented language to graduate the workshop.
    • Wharton MBA Challenge: Fourth and fifth graders are required to pass the Wharton MBA simulation challenge (which 50% of adult MBAs fail) as part of their core requirements.
  • Scaling with Quality: Since taking over as principal 4 years ago, Liemandt has productized the school model, scaling from Austin to 50 campuses while test scores, student happiness, and workshop quality improve annually.

Reinventing Higher Education & the HAA Model

  • The Broken University Format: Speaking to visiting interns from MIT, Stanford, and UT, Liemandt found that only 1 student out of more than 70 felt their university was properly preparing them for post-graduation life in the age of AI. Large lecture classes have attendance dropping below 10%, with students viewing them as a charade.
  • Horowitz Andreessen Academy (HAA) Design Principles: Gagan Biyani explains that HAA applies similar modern principles to college-age students by focusing heavily on student success rather than adult politics.
    • The 80-Hour Internship Test: Summer interns at Alpha worked 80 hours a week researching learning science and building educational small language models (SLMs) to make them free for global sovereigns, proving that motivated students thrive when building real products.
    • High-Ambition Travel and Autonomy: HAA allocates $5,000 per student for travel budgets, encouraging solo travel to countries with less than $20,000 GDP per capita to build global perspective and resilience.
  • The Value of Network and Proximity: Drawing inspiration from early institutions like the Teal Fellowship, HAA curates its applicant pool tightly, exposing students to legendary builders (such as Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, and Satya Nadella) to raise their personal ambitions.

Entrepreneurship and the Future of Work

  • Founder School: Alpha launched a specialized high school focused entirely on entrepreneurship, recognizing that AI will drive a massive explosion in independent business creation.
  • The Million-Dollar Guarantee: Founder School guarantees that students will start a business earning $1 million in profit while in high school, or tuition is refunded. Students are currently speed-running the curriculum as freshmen.
  • The Power of Cold Outreach: Highlighting student agency, Liemandt shared the story of a 14-year-old student who cold-called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. While Huang critiqued the student's call preparation (giving him an "F" on research), he took the call and gave him mentorship—turning it into a transformative life lesson.

Overcoming Parental Resistance and Cultural Inertia

  • The 1910 Farm Tractor Analogy: Liemandt compares the current educational inflection point to 1910, when the introduction of the farm tractor made 30% of agricultural jobs obsolete, prompting 130,000 American towns to vote to raise taxes to fund a brand-new high school system.
  • Adoption Curves: Opening new campuses often starts with small cohorts (e.g., opening New York City with 10 to 12 students), but demand skyrockets once local families witness the actual performance and happiness of the first cohorts.
  • Product Definition: Liemandt stresses that schools must clearly define their product—attracting families who embrace modern tools and repelling laggards who reject screens or AI.

TL;DR

Scott Kirby, CEO of United Airlines, details the airline’s contrarian pandemic strategy of massive fleet and technology expansion, the rollout of SpaceX Starlink across every plane, and why customer surveys and traditional metrics fail in the airline business.

Fleet Expansion & Contrarian Bets

  • Pandemic Wide-Body Order: During COVID when travel experts predicted demand would drop 50% forever and global competitors permanently retired wide-body fleets, Scott Kirby and United did the opposite, executing the largest aircraft order in history: 200 wide-bodies and several hundred narrow-bodies.
  • Capital Discipline vs. Short-Termism: United invested heavily during the downturn to secure 30-year assets at advantageous pricing, mirroring cyclical manufacturing strategies like Samsung's memory investments.
  • Market Dominance in Hubs: Scott Kirby highlights that single-hub operations (like Atlanta and Dallas) drive more international service and economic activity than fragmented hubs like Chicago, where United and American Airlines duplicate 16 daily flights to Milwaukee.

Technology Stack & In-House Software

  • Core Tech Modernization: In 2020, United invested hundreds of millions to move off mainframes onto the cloud and build modern databases, enabling fast execution that competitors cannot replicate.
  • In-House Reservation Legacy: United is one of only two airlines globally (alongside Copa Airlines) that owns its own reservation system, refusing to outsource to Sabre or Apollo.
  • Seat-Back Map & Entertainment Redesign: United is taking over map software from Panasonic to eliminate annoying globe views and build personalized preferences and proactive milestone memories (such as a live countdown to a passenger's 2 millionth mile).
  • AI Vibe Coding: After taking three 1-hour tutoring sessions, Scott Kirby independently wrote a sports betting aggregation web app in 2.5 hours at his home gym, sparking an internal AI push.

Starlink Rollout & Competitive Differentiation

  • Speed Over "Free": United chose SpaceX's Starlink not because it is free, but because fast bandwidth is the true value proposition; legacy free Wi-Fi is compared to slow dial-up internet.
  • Fleet Rollout Pace: United is currently at 48% of flights equipped with Starlink, upgrading about three planes per day and planning to reach 50% within a week and 100% in hubs like Los Angeles in the first half of next year.
  • Targeting Competitors: Scott Kirby views Starlink as a temporary multi-year competitive advantage that will drive passengers from competing airlines (including Delta and joint-venture partner ANA) to try United and stay for its superior overall technology.

Operational Hurdles & Air Traffic Control

  • ATC as the Primary Bottleneck: Air traffic control accounts for 90% of airline operational issues, constrained by inefficient annual appropriations processes and political distribution of 450 regional facilities.
  • Weather Simulation: United is using AI simulations for Denver summer pop-up thunderstorms to potentially reduce weather-impacted delays by 50%–75%.
  • Low-Cost Carrier Failures: Low-cost carriers like Spirit Airlines failed because cost inflation and exorbitant airport authority fees (such as $52 per passenger in New York airports) made their business model mathematically unsustainable.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Hub-Specific Starlink Target: Scott Kirby stated that Los Angeles will be United's first 100% Starlink-equipped hub in the first half of next year.
  • Weather Delay Reductions: Scott Kirby claimed that AI simulations can reduce weather-impacted delays in Denver by 50% to 75% in the summer.
  • Industry Financial Outlook: Scott Kirby predicted that 6 out of 10 US airlines will lose money this year.

For political reasons. It makes it incredibly inefficient. One wire gets cut, and if you got one big facility, you get a backup. As we saw. You have 450 of them. Things happen all the time. It just makes the system inefficient. I'm not actually advocating for privatizing the FAA, because it's so politically toxic. You didn't have to be a rocket scientist to figure out if you're paying $52 out of $58 before you buy your fuel, before you buy your airplanes, before you pay your employees, before you do maintenance, that just mathematically doesn't work. The airport authorities... The big airports in the country are up something like 70% of the expenses since pre-COVID to today. They've just priced low-cost carriers out of the market. Well, did you price low-cost carriers out of the market? We didn't price them out. You had the basic level, and you had this much more fine-grained cutting up of the seats. The low-cost carrier business model was predicated on having a price advantage. Being able to charge a lower price. We created basic economy where we could profit. And we up-gauged airplanes, so we could profitably be competitive on price most of the time. If we're competitive on price, there's no reason... My joke was: "People may make the mistake of flying Spirit once, but they're not going to do it twice." Why did Spirit go bust? Because they weren't charging as much as their costs. They were not able to charge enough— That's what I'm trying to ask— It's pretty simple. It was simple. They weren't able to charge enough. Look, what's happening— It was because of cost inflation, basically. Cost inflation, but there's a whole bunch of things. Fundamentally, what I think has happened to the low-cost carriers... There's really one still low-cost carrier, successful airline in the world. It's Ryanair. I was going to ask. The fundamental premise of a low-cost carrier is to fly to low-cost airports. Southwest, when they started flying here, they flew to Oakland, not San Francisco. San Francisco is too expensive. In LA, they didn't fly to LAX. They flew to Burbank and Ontario. LAX is too expensive. Ryanair still does it. Ryanair doesn't fly to Heathrow. They don't fly to Charles de Gaulle. They fly to secondary airports, because they're low-cost. All these companies' eyes get too big for their— In the US, every single one of them abandoned that. Is it an ego? Then they went to fly into… I don't know why. They run out of customers, right? Yeah, and they went into Chicago and Newark and San Francisco. Back to the New York... You can't charge 58 bucks when you're paying the airport authority 52. You just can't. Is it a chasing growth story? I'm always very impressed by In-N-Out as a business because they don't chase growth. They famously do everything within one day's drive of the refrigeration centers... Distribution centers. And so they're only in the California West Coast type area. They don't feel the desire to go crazy on the menu: "We have the salad this, and we have whatever that." I see they keep the menu very narrow. I feel like maybe if they're a public company, they were trying to chase growth, and we're going to expand this way. And they just do the same thing exceptionally well with a cost advantage. Is the problem that as public companies, maybe, or as just short-term oriented companies, they had this good thing flying to Oakland and flying to the secondary airports, and for whatever reason, they just got distracted from it? Yeah, I would actually say a little different than just chasing growth. I would say, know who you are, know what your strengths are, and stick to your knitting. Companies are not good at trying to be something they're not. In the past, this predated me, but all the big airlines, American, Delta, Northwest, Continental, tried to go compete with Southwest by creating airlines within an airline that were going to try to out-Southwest Southwest. In Europe, they still do it. In Asia, they still do it. They try to out-low-cost carry low-cost carry. And they're terrible at it! Every single one of them has been. Nobody does it well. By the way, Southwest has now tried to be like us. They're not going to be very good at that either. You got to stick to the things that you're good at. We aren't going to ever go try to compete with Allegiant Air and be Allegiant Air because we'd be terrible. They're better at Allegiant. If they try to compete with us— The low-cost model works, but you have to understand. You got to stick to it. You got to accept that there's limitations. "I'm not going to be as big as United Airlines. I'm not going to fly to Chicago O'Hare." I have a great… Allegiant is an example. Allegiant Air, you know, it mostly flies to Vegas. They fly from small cities. They've done a great... They're one of the four airlines that is going to be profitable this year. What else have you learned from Ryanair? The guy's entertaining. Michael O'Leary is entertaining. We'd like to get him in the pub here. You had him here? No, I would like to. You'll get a few more swear words than you get him out of me. He knows his business exceptionally well. He's a very impressive CEO. They're also In-N-Out. They have avoided distraction. He's disciplined. They always get asked about transatlantic. Discipline is probably a better way. It doesn't work because you don't get the low-cost advantage when you can't get the number of turns high enough. They get asked about Wi-Fi on the planes, and it's like, "Guys, the flights are short. Just look at your phone for an hour or something. You don't need it on an hour-long flight." He's disciplined. That's a better way of saying it. Getting outside, you have to be disciplined to be successful. Companies get stars in their eyes, and they're not disciplined. What's the version of discipline for you? Because it's easy, like United, you guys are a huge global airline. You fly big aircraft, you fly small aircraft, you fly internationally, you fly domestically. It would be easy to want to do everything where it's like, "We're cost-competitive, but we have a great wine list." What is your version of staying disciplined? In the airline business, discipline is really about where you fly. The foundation, our product starts with the route network— You fly routes that make money— And fly places that make money. Every time I go— Does that mean where you're less point-to-point in domestics? We don't fly point-to-point. I hear it all the time. In LA yesterday, when I do stuff in San Francisco tomorrow with employees, they're always asking, wanting to fly new routes and point-to-point routes. It won't work for us. We're an airline that flies to our hubs. We fly to our hubs. That's our strength and a whole bunch of reasons that works. We're not going to go try to fly point-to-point routes. If you're not first, you're last. If you're not first, you're last. That's true in the airline business. It's by market. It's not overall. People in Dallas ask me, "Why do you not fly here?" Because we'd lose. American has too much network depth. When they fly from Dallas to Los Angeles, 75% of the people on the airplane are connecting from other destinations. If we're just flying Dallas and LA, we can't compete because we don't have any connections. We're competing for 25% of the market. It doesn't work. Does that then mean the little decisions you make are, "Okay, should we fly from, is it Newark to Greenland?" That's a little decision. The big decision is: "Are we going to launch a beachhead and take a new hub?" How frequently do you make those decisions? Rarely. Is the last big hub up, Denver, when you grew it hugely? But this was an existing hub that we chose to grow. In my 30-year career, I've closed three hubs and never opened a new one. It's a hard decision to do. It's very rare that that's… Lots of examples in the airline industry of that not working, and almost none of that working in the post-deregulation era. Do you think it's basically impossible to launch a new hub these days? Building a new airport, it just hasn't happened in the last 50 years. Yes, is the short answer. Take the Southeast. It's the one part of the country where we're number three because Delta has a hub in Atlanta, American has a hub in Charlotte. I'd like us to be bigger in the Southeast, and it doesn't matter to customers, but there's just simply no airport that's big enough where we can be competitive. We would need to have 600 flights a day to be competitive with American and Delta. The biggest city that would work, that's a big enough city, maybe is Raleigh-Durham. But the airport's not big enough. There aren't enough gates. There aren't enough runways. You couldn't have 600 flights a day. Try to do something just because it's a cool vision, we don't do. We're disciplined. But this would be a big enough deal for a region that could you work with Raleigh-Durham to expand the airport? Expanding airports in this country is like... A decade-long process. Yeah, more. That's optimistic, probably. Okay, so you think it's just—It's just… Okay, so discipline for you— It's possible someday we'll at least experiment with going into a big city that's not really a hub for anyone. Delta has done some of that. It's been, I think, break-evenish, but they've not lost money. You did, though. This is not a hub at all, but way back in the day, you used to have a hub in Narita. You've added a few connecting flights. There's one from Hong Kong to Thailand and to Vietnam— Ulaanbaatar— And you're flying to Kaohsiung from Narita now. Is that just more on the margins sort of things? It's on the margins, but there are places like in Tokyo, we have connectivity with our partner. A lot of the people that… Like Ulaanbaatar, we realized that something like 12% of the people that were flying us into Tokyo were ultimately trying to get to Ulaanbaatar, and it was really hard. ANA didn't fly there. That is a mess. Wait, I don't believe that— What's going on here— That number is way too high. It was the summer, but it was a high percentage of people. For vacation? Yeah. Am I missing something? I haven't been to Ulaanbaatar. Am I missing anything? I haven't been there either. My mom went. My mom travels a lot. She uses my flight benefits and travels a lot. She's just awesome. But... We've seen that data and we added the flight. Now a lot of the people that fly us into Tokyo connect on to Ulaanbaatar. It was a particular flight that it was 12% at one time a day, at that time of day. But then we also have all the ANA connections. They weren't flying. Kaohsiung is the same thing. For us—Why to Sapporo? It's going to be fun. Sapporo is booking really well. It's going to be… Is that for skiing? Skiing. Yeah. But Japan has become like... The hottest destination— For the tech people here in San Francisco. People just love it. Even in Dallas, people love Japan. I have all kinds of friends that, "We went to Japan for spring break," and they love the food, the people are great. They just love it. What I'm taking away from this is that route selection makes or breaks airlines. Yes. It broke Spirit or the low-cost carriers. It broke American in this fracas you guys had. Well, they haven't accepted that it broke them, but it did. Then similarly, success means a disciplined route expansion strategy that understands your strengths. Look, that's pretty insightful. I tell new CEOs, which many of them call, talk to me. I don't think any of them have taken my advice yet, but I tell them, "The one thing I'll tell you, start with the route network is the foundation. If that's broken, it doesn't matter how good you do everything else. If you have bad routes that lose money, you cannot make the airline work. It is impossible." You're going to hear, if you look through the route P&L, which you should do, you're going to see a bunch of negative flying. When you ask people about it, they're going to say it's strategic. They're going to have convincing excuses. They're going to call it strategic. If you hear the word strategic flying, you don't need to know what hub it is, you don't need to know what route it is, you should cancel it. You have to stop flying. Anything that... If you default to it loses money, but it's strategic, you have to cancel it. And they don't do it. What are the lies people tell themselves to convince themselves to stay running a route? What does it mean to be strategic? Corporate customers, something like that. Yeah, or credit cards. If we're not big in this city, then we just won't get the credit card— Is that the biggest tail risk if credit cards ever go away? No, it's not nearly as big as people think. The perception amongst the— Yeah, the perception is big because people look at… They can see the amount of revenue that we get, and they say, "Oh, almost all your net profit is coming from credit cards." Well, yeah, but there's a cost. We carry over 50,000 people a day. 50,000 people today will fly free on United Airlines by using their credit card miles. Nobody counts the cost. Oh, you're saying they just can't do an accurate contribution profit calculation? Yes. All that we disclose is the revenue. Everyone's like, "Oh, look at the revenue." Fifty thousand people a day are flying for free. There's a cost of carrying 50,000 people. Okay, so the whole Twitter meme of airlines are a credit card business with airplanes attached, it's just they're holding the financial statement upside down. They're ignoring half. They're looking at the revenue side and ignoring the cost. Ignoring the cost side. It's important. It's good, but— But it's blown way out of proportion. But it's blown way out of proportion— How do you think about changes in the frequent flyer program? You just went to, I think, $32,000 or whatever you call it—points—which... I appreciate getting rid of the segment one because I never qualified on that one, so I appreciate the simplification. But, is that a— You in general just seem to want to keep the riffraff out, like with the Wi-Fi, with the… It's a real challenge here. They want the cutoff to be right below Ben. Yeah. That's exactly right. I applaud these changes. I looked back on my past few years. I've always well-exceeded 32,000, so it's no problem for me. I want emptier lounges, so it's all good. What's the calculation in that? Delta obviously has gotten a lot of grief from my frequent flyers in the changes they made. Yours seemed to go fairly well. What do you think that was? I don't think about it through the lens of the frequent flyer program. I think about how do we grow brand loyalty. The frequent flyer program is one of those things. Really, if we're doing something that's going to detract from brand loyalty, there's got to be a good reason to do it. Clubs are… How many people are a Global Services member? People love being Global Services, but we limit it. It's exclusive. There was one year I thought I was going to make it. January passed and it never came. It was very sad. Clubs are another example. This is another thing. During COVID, I'm pretty sure we're the only airline that did this, we doubled down on club investment. We've doubled our square footage of club space from pre-COVID to more than doubled it. And it's going to grow by another 50%. It was the one time in history... If you close a club, it's complicated. But close a club, it makes customers mad in the short term. You have to do it sometimes to expand it. But COVID was the one time in history, we had to spend money, but we had no customers. We could get away with doing it, we could do it faster. Expanding club space is what we have a bit. We're going to do more of that. Those are the kinds of things that we're more focused on. Any changes to the frequent flyer program are about trying to build loyalty. That is just, "We could deliver a better experience if there's fewer people." Well, sometimes it's that. I guess there's only a certain number. We're putting more first-class seats on, but at any given time, we only have so many first-class seats on airplanes. We're calibrating the program to make it valuable for loyal customers. You run the Star Alliance board? Not anymore. Oh, you used to. What's that like? Because it's an interesting construct, right? It's one of these businesses where the airline business is one of these businesses where these are kind of competitors, but you do run some overlapping routes, but it's better to work together, but then you got to pick who you work together with. How much are you picking based on the vibe of the other CEO versus it's strategic? How much does that change? We're all locked into alliances now. It's hard to switch. The real value for customers is being able to connect on to places that we don't fly to. When we fly, we fly into Frankfurt and Munich, and I think we have four times as many flights into Frankfurt and Munich as American and Delta combined. But it's because we have a partnership with Lufthansa. I think 60% of the people on our Frankfurt and Munich flights are connecting beyond Munich. They're going to Kazakhstan and all kinds of places that we don't fly to. That's the value for customers. The downside is the experience doesn't feel the same as on United. That's what we've been working to do. We've made a lot of progress. That got everyone to do it. We've been begging them to do it for years, but it just wasn't a priority for them. Other stuff wasn't their priority. We finally had to say, "We're going to cut you off unless you do it." My focus on our partnerships has been, how do we make the customer... If a United customer is flying on any of our partners, how do we make it feel to them like it is still United Airlines? I think the other airlines ought to be doing this— Is that the nature of the partnership? You provide the most customers, and so that ultimately gives you the control— Yeah, we're by far the biggest and the access to have the big hubs. Lufthansa is second. Across the Pacific, ANA is big. There's just several big partners. But some of the others are like, one of my favorite airlines is Croatia. I love the people. They're small touring airplanes. One, I love Croatia. It's a great country. Super fun. People are awesome. I like the CEO. I like the culture. I like the people. It doesn't drive a ton of economic value, but when we try to do new stuff, if we're going to do new technology stuff, they're one of the smallest. They raise their hand every time. So, I appreciate that. Your career is very much defined by consolidation and doing stuff together. You've been talking about, "Oh, we should just buy American Airlines or whatever it might be." Is there any limit in your belief in the power of consolidation and doing a better consumer experience? But, in non-commodity businesses, doing things that are good for your customers is the winning formula. The consolidation that—I actually hadn't thought about this. The consolidation dynamic that you're referencing is that ultimately, eliminating duplicative flights in a capacity-constrained airport, which is all the major ones, means that you can have more selection as a— That's the Chicago example. That they think of as the flag carrier of the United States. If you go to Dubai, people are proud of Emirates. They may complain about stuff, but they're proud of Emirates. By the way, that doesn't create as many good jobs in the US. It's a whole bunch of reasons. Traders Brace for Fed Day
